def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-prio.claim:
For type S use a fixed sufficiently regular compactly supported orthonormal multiresolution wavelet basis $(\psi_{lk})$ on $[0,1]$ as in [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]], with boundary correction, regularity greater than the truth smoothness $\alpha$, and $|K_l|=2^l$. The spaces $V_L$ spanned by the retained levels $l\le L$ contain constants and have orthonormal scaling bases with uniformly bounded overlap, support diameters at most $C2^{-L}$, and suprema at most $C2^{L/2}$; a fixed shift of the scaling-resolution index is absorbed in $C$. The wavelets likewise have uniformly bounded overlap, support diameters at most $C2^{-l}$, and suprema at most $C2^{l/2}$. For an integer $m>\alpha$, the detail wavelets have vanishing moments through degree $m-1$, and derivatives through order $m$ satisfy $\|\psi_{lk}^{(q)}\|_\infty\le C_q2^{l(q+1/2)}$, with uniformly bounded overlap of their supports; the fixed low scaling functions are $C^m$. These are the sufficiently regular compact multiresolution basis conditions in the source density theorem. For the density-model source results, every truth $f_0$ is a probability density satisfying $0<\rho_0\le f_0\le D_0<\infty$ for constants $\rho_0,D_0$. For $n\ge3$ and smoothness index $\alpha>0$, let $j_n$ and $\ell_n$ be the largest integers satisfying
$$2^{j_n}\le n^{1/(2\alpha+1)},\qquad 2^{\ell_n}\le(n/\log n)^{1/(2\alpha+1)}.$$
Choose one cutoff sequence $L_n\in\{j_n,\ell_n\}$ for all $n\ge3$; set any finite $L_n$ for $n=1,2$, which does not change asymptotic claims.

For a finite wavelet series $T_n=\sum_{l\le L_n}\sum_{k\in K_l}\sigma_l\xi_{lk}\psi_{lk}$, define $c(T_n)=\log\int_0^1e^{T_n(x)}dx$ and the normalized log-density $f_n(x)=e^{T_n(x)-c(T_n)}$.

The **type-S1 family** takes IID coefficients $\xi_{lk}$ with a continuous density $\varphi_H$ for which $\log\varphi_H$ is Lipschitz, and uses $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$. Its source theorem assumes $\log f_0$ has coefficient Hölder regularity $\alpha>1$ and $f_0$ is bounded above and bounded away from zero.

The **type-S2 family** takes IID standard-normal coefficients and uses $\sigma_l=2^{-l(r+1/2)}$, where $0<r<\alpha-1/4$; its source theorem uses $\log f_0\in C^\alpha$, $\alpha>1/2$, and positive finite density bounds.

For the **type-H family**, use the Haar basis instead of the regular type-S wavelets: its scaling function is $1$ and $\psi_{lk}=2^{l/2}(1_{I_{l+1,2k}}-1_{I_{l+1,2k+1}})$ for $l\ge0$ and $0\le k<2^l$. The histogram space at resolution $L$ consists of the scaling coordinate and detail levels $l<L$; all detail coefficients at $l\ge L$ vanish. Partition $[0,1]$ into dyadic cells $I_{L_n,k}$ of length $2^{-L_n}$, draw $\omega=(\omega_k)_{k<2^{L_n}}\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(a_{0,L_n},\ldots,a_{2^{L_n}-1,L_n})$, and set $f_n=2^{L_n}\omega_k$ on cell $I_{L_n,k}$. The source assumptions are $c_1 2^{-L_na}\le a_{k,L_n}\le c_2$ for fixed positive $a,c_1,c_2$, and $f_0\in C^\alpha$ for $1/2<\alpha\le1$, together with the common positive finite density bounds above. The posterior asymptotic conclusions for these families are separate results.

Here $C^\alpha_\psi$ denotes the coefficient class with norm $\|g\|_{C^\alpha_\psi}:=\sup_{l,k}2^{l(\alpha+1/2)}|\langle g,\psi_{lk}\rangle|$. For sufficiently regular standard wavelets this is the usual Hölder scale (with the usual Zygmund interpretation at integer smoothness).

derivations.claim: Let $(x^{(m)})$ be Cauchy in $M_0(w)$. Each coordinate is Cauchy because $|x^{(m)}_{lk}-x^{(n)}_{lk}|\le w_l\|x^{(m)}-x^{(n)}\|_{M(w)}$. Let $x_{lk}$ be its scalar limit. The uniform Cauchy bound passes to every finite collection of coordinates and then to the supremum, so $x^{(m)}\to x$ in the weighted supremum norm. To see $x\in M_0(w)$, fix $\varepsilon>0$, choose $m$ with $\|x-x^{(m)}\|_{M(w)}<\varepsilon$, then choose $J$ so the normalized tail of $x^{(m)}$ is below $\varepsilon$; for $l>J$ the normalized tail of $x$ is at most $2\varepsilon$. Thus $M_0(w)$ is complete.

Finite-support sequences with rational coordinates are countable and dense: first choose $J$ to make the tail of any $x\in M_0(w)$ small, then approximate its finitely many coordinates through level $J$ by rationals. Hence $M_0(w)$ is separable. The formula for the norm shows $P_J$ is a contraction, and the defining tail limit gives $\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\to0$.

If $x\in\ell^2$, then $w_l\ge1$ implies $w_l^{-1}\max_k|x_{lk}|\le(\sum_k|x_{lk}|^2)^{1/2}$. The right side tends to zero because its squares are level blocks of a convergent nonnegative series. Its supremum is at most $\|x\|_{\ell^2}$, so $x\in M_0(w)$.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

derivations.claim: For fixed $t$ and level $l\ge l_0$, a wavelet whose support lies wholly on one side of $t$ contributes zero: it is either disjoint from $[0,t]$ or its entire support is integrated and its mean is zero. Only supports meeting $t$ can contribute. Uniformly bounded overlap bounds their number by a constant, and each coefficient has magnitude at most $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C_0 2^{-l/2}$. Thus $\sup_t\sum_k|\langle1_{[0,t]},\psi_{lk}\rangle|\le C_1 2^{-l/2}$. The finitely many coarsest levels have a finite uniform sum as well.

By [F1] and step 1.1, the absolute sum of all terms at levels $l\ge l_0$ is at most $C_1\|x\|_{M(w)}\sum_{l\ge l_0}w_l2^{-l/2}$, uniformly over $t$. Its tails tend uniformly to zero because $S_w<\infty$. Each finite-level sum is continuous in $t$, since $t\mapsto\int_0^t\psi_{lk}(u)du$ is continuous for an $L^1$ function. The uniform limit is continuous. Applying the same estimate to $x-y$ proves the stated operator-norm bound.

If $x_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$ for $f\in L^2$, the finite orthogonal projections converge to $f$ in $L^2$ by [F2]. The map $f\mapsto\int_0^t f(u)du=\langle f,1_{[0,t]}\rangle$ is a continuous $L^2$ functional because $\|1_{[0,t]}\|_2\le1$. lem-multiscale-primitive-map-to-continuo.claim:
Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a compactly supported wavelet basis of [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The Haar basis with its finite scaling coordinate, as specified in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], is also allowed. Assume each level-$l$ wavelet for $l\ge l_0$ has zero integral, uniformly bounded overlap, support length at most $C_0 2^{-l}$, and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C_0 2^{-l/2}$. Let $M_0(w)$ be as in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and suppose
$$S_w:=\sum_{l\ge l_0}w_l2^{-l/2}<\infty.$$
For $x\in M_0(w)$ define
$$Jx(t):=\sum_{l,k}x_{lk}\langle 1_{[0,t]},\psi_{lk}\rangle_{L^2},\qquad 0\le t\le1.$$
Then this series converges absolutely and uniformly in $t$, $Jx\in C([0,1])$, and $\|Jx-Jy\|_\infty\le C S_w\|x-y\|_{M(w)}$ after adding the finite coarsest-level constant to $C S_w$. If $x$ is the coefficient sequence of $f\in L^2$, then $Jx(t)=\int_0^t f(u)\,du$.

$$H^s_2=\left\{g\in L^2([0,1]):\sum_{l,k}a_l^{2s}|\langle g,\psi_{lk}\rangle|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For $g\in H^s_2$, $s>1/2$, and $f\in L^2([0,1])$, define $L_g(f)=\langle f,g\rangle_{L^2}$. For $x=(x_{lk})\in H(\delta)$, the intended extension is the coefficient pairing $L_g(x)=\sum_{l,k}x_{lk}\langle g,\psi_{lk}\rangle$; [[lem-smooth-functional-extends-to-negative-sobolev-space]] proves that this series is absolutely convergent and defines a continuous linear functional on $H(\delta)$ for every $\delta>0$.

In the white-noise experiment $X^{(n)}=f_0+n^{-1/2}W$, $L_g(X^{(n)})$ means this continuous pairing with the $H(\delta)$-valued observation. It does not assert that $X^{(n)}$ is an $L^2$ function. The representer is nonzero when $g\ne0$; the corresponding white-noise variance is $\|g\|_2^2$.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. Their inner products with $g$ are the finite partial sums of the displayed pairing, and converge to $\langle f,g\rangle_{L^2}$ by continuity of the inner product. $$2^{j_n}\le n^{1/(2\alpha+1)},\qquad 2^{\ell_n}\le(n/\log n)^{1/(2\alpha+1)}.$$

The **type-S1 family** takes IID coefficients $\xi_{lk}$ with a continuous density $\varphi_H$ for which $\log\varphi_H$ is Lipschitz, and uses $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$. Its source theorem assumes $\log f_0$ has coefficient Hölder regularity $\alpha>1$ and $f_0$ is bounded above and bounded away from zero.

The **type-S2 family** takes IID standard-normal coefficients and uses $\sigma_l=2^{-l(r+1/2)}$, where $0<r<\alpha-1/4$; its source theorem uses $\log f_0\in C^\alpha$, $\alpha>1/2$, and positive finite density bounds.

For the **type-H family**, use the Haar basis instead of the regular type-S wavelets: its scaling function is $1$ and $\psi_{lk}=2^{l/2}(1_{I_{l+1,2k}}-1_{I_{l+1,2k+1}})$ for $l\ge0$ and $0\le k<2^l$. $$M(w)=\left\{x=(x_{lk}):\|x\|_{M(w)}:=\sup_l\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}<\infty\right\}$$
and its closed little-o subspace
$$M_0(w)=\left\{x\in M(w):\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}\longrightarrow0\text{ as }l\to\infty\right\},$$
with the same norm. Call $w$ admissible when $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. The finite coarsest level is included in the norm and does not affect this limit. Elements are coefficient sequences; in particular, they need not be $L^2$ functions. [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]] proves that $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space, that $L^2$ coefficient sequences embed in it, and that finite-level projections converge in its norm.

$$\beta_{BL}(Q_n\circ P_J^{-1},G\circ P_J^{-1})\to0$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

Fix $J$. For all sufficiently large $n$, $L_n\ge J$, so the coordinates of $P_JU_n$ are $n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n(\psi_{lk}(X_i)-P_0\psi_{lk})$ for the finitely many indices through level $J$. The vector summand is bounded by [A2], has finite second moment, and is IID by [F9]; its covariance is the displayed covariance of $G_{P_0}$. By [F4] these finite-dimensional vectors converge weakly to the corresponding Gaussian projection. The projection space is finite-dimensional Euclidean with an equivalent weighted maximum norm, so [F5] gives convergence in bounded-Lipschitz distance for every fixed $J$.

Let $Y_i=\psi_{lk}(X_i)-P_0\psi_{lk}$. Then $\mathbb EY_i=0$, $\mathbb EY_i^2\le P_0\psi_{lk}^2\le B$, and $|Y_i|\le2C_0 2^{l/2}=:b_l$ by [A2]. For $m\ge2$, $\mathbb E|Y_i|^m\le b_l^{m-2}\mathbb EY_i^2$. Since $m!\ge2\,3^{m-2}$, expansion of the exponential gives, for $0<\lambda b_l<3\sqrt n$, $\mathbb E\exp(\lambda n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i)\le\exp(\lambda^2B/[2(1-\lambda b_l/(3\sqrt n))])$. Applying [F7] to this exponential and optimizing at $\lambda=t/(B+b_lt/(3\sqrt n))$ yields $P_0^n\{|\sqrt n(P_n-P_0)\psi_{lk}|>t\}\le2\exp(-t^2/[2(B+b_lt/(3\sqrt n))])$. Applying the same argument to $-Y_i$ supplies the lower-tail bound.

Above the cutoff, $U_n$ has only the deterministic bias coefficients $-\sqrt n\langle f_0,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. By [A3] and monotonicity of $w_l$, $\sup_{l>L_n,k}\sqrt n|\langle f_0,\psi_{lk}\rangle|/w_l\le C_f\sqrt n\,2^{-L_n(\gamma+1/2)}/w_{L_n}$. For the first cutoff regime the numerator is bounded, while $w_{L_n}\to\infty$. For the second, the numerator is $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ and $\sqrt{L_n}\asymp\sqrt{\log n}$; admissibility $w_{L_n}/\sqrt{L_n}\to\infty$ again makes the ratio vanish.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By [F6] and step 1.3, $P_0^n\{\max_{J<l\le L_n,k}|\sqrt n(P_n-P_0)\psi_{lk}|/w_l>\varepsilon\}\le\sum_{J<l\le L_n}2^{l+1}\exp(-\varepsilon^2w_l^2/[2(B+(2C_0\varepsilon/3)2^{l/2}w_l/\sqrt n)])$. For levels with $2^{l/2}w_l/\sqrt n\le1$, the denominator is bounded by a constant depending only on $B,C_0,\varepsilon$. Their sum is bounded by $\sum_{l>J}2^{l+1}e^{-c_\varepsilon w_l^2}$, which tends to zero as $J\to\infty$: admissibility gives $w_l^2/l\to\infty$, so the summand is eventually bounded by $2^{-l}$.

For the remaining levels $2^{l/2}w_l/\sqrt n>1$, the exponent in step 2.1 is at least $c_\varepsilon w_l\sqrt n/2^{l/2}\ge c_\varepsilon\sqrt n/2^{L_n/2}$. Their total contribution is at most $2^{L_n+2}\exp(-c_\varepsilon\sqrt n/2^{L_n/2})$, which tends to zero. Indeed $L_n=O(\log n)$ and either cutoff gives $\sqrt n/2^{L_n/2}\ge c n^{\gamma/(2\gamma+1)}$ for all large $n$ after decreasing $c>0$ if needed; this polynomial growth dominates $L_n\log2$.

The two threshold classes partition all levels $J<l\le L_n$. The low-threshold sum tends to zero as $J\to\infty$ by step 2.1, and the high-threshold sum tends to zero as $n\to\infty$ by step 3.1. Therefore the centered empirical-fluctuation tails vanish in the iterated limit $n\to\infty$, then $J\to\infty$.

For the fixed Gaussian law $G_{P_0}$, [F2] gives $\|G_{P_0}-P_JG_{P_0}\|_{M(w)}\to0$ pointwise. Hence the events $\{\|G_{P_0}-P_JG_{P_0}\|_{M(w)}>\varepsilon\}$ decrease to the empty set; [F8] makes their probabilities tend to zero. Steps 4.1 and 1.4 give the matching posterior-tail condition for the laws of $U_n$.

For each fixed $J$, step 1.2 gives convergence of the projected laws in bounded-Lipschitz distance; steps 4.1 and 1.4 give vanishing tails for $U_n$, and step 5.1 gives vanishing tails for $G_{P_0}$. Applying [F3] to these laws proves $\beta_{BL}(\mathcal L(U_n),G_{P_0})\to0$, which is the asserted weak convergence on $M_0(w)$.

Use the wavelet coefficient levels $(l,k)$ and multiplicities $|K_l|=2^l$ from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The same coefficient-space definition applies to the Haar system used for type-H histograms: detail levels $l\ge0$ have $2^l$ coefficients, and the single scaling coefficient is an additional finite coarsest coordinate, included in the norm with weight $1$. Finite projections always retain that scaling coordinate; this finite convention does not alter any tail assertion. Let $w=(w_l)$ be nondecreasing with $w_l\ge1$. Define
$$M(w)=\left\{x=(x_{lk}):\|x\|_{M(w)}:=\sup_l\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}<\infty\right\}$$
and its closed little-o subspace
$$M_0(w)=\left\{x\in M(w):\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}\longrightarrow0\text{ as }l\to\infty\right\},$$
with the same norm. Call $w$ admissible when $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. The finite coarsest level is included in the norm and does not affect this limit. Elements are coefficient sequences; in particular, they need not be $L^2$ functions. [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]] proves that $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space, that $L^2$ coefficient sequences embed in it, and that finite-level projections converge in its norm.

For every weight sequence in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space. If $P_J$ retains exactly the coefficients at levels $l\le J$, then $\|P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\le\|x\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\to0$ for each $x\in M_0(w)$. Every square-summable coefficient sequence belongs to $M_0(w)$.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a compactly supported wavelet basis of [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The Haar basis with its finite scaling coordinate, as specified in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], is also allowed. Assume each level-$l$ wavelet for $l\ge l_0$ has zero integral, uniformly bounded overlap, support length at most $C_0 2^{-l}$, and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C_0 2^{-l/2}$. Let $M_0(w)$ be as in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and suppose
$$S_w:=\sum_{l\ge l_0}w_l2^{-l/2}<\infty.$$
For $x\in M_0(w)$ define
$$Jx(t):=\sum_{l,k}x_{lk}\langle 1_{[0,t]},\psi_{lk}\rangle_{L^2},\qquad 0\le t\le1.$$
Then this series converges absolutely and uniformly in $t$, $Jx\in C([0,1])$, and $\|Jx-Jy\|_\infty\le C S_w\|x-y\|_{M(w)}$ after adding the finite coarsest-level constant to $C S_w$. If $x$ is the coefficient sequence of $f\in L^2$, then $Jx(t)=\int_0^t f(u)\,du$.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

Write $\mathbb Q$ for the canonical image of the rationals in $\mathbb R$ under the embedding of [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]].

Let $y\mapsto\Pi_y$ be a probability kernel on $\mathbb R$. For $u\in(0,1)$ put
$$F_y(t)=\Pi_y((-\infty,t]),\qquad q_u(y)=\inf\{r\in\mathbb Q:F_y(r)\ge u\}.$$The infimum is taken in $\mathbb R$; [[thm-infimum-property]] supplies it once the defining set is shown nonempty and bounded below. Then $q_u:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, and$$\Pi_y((-\infty,q_u(y)))\le u\le\Pi_y((-\infty,q_u(y)]).$$

Let $Q_n(y,\cdot)$ be data-indexed probability kernels on $\mathbb R$, let $Q$ be a fixed law with continuous CDF $F$, and suppose $\beta_{BL}(Q_n(y,\cdot),Q)\to0$ in probability. Fix $0<u<1$ and let $q=q_u(Q):=\inf\{r\in\mathbb Q:Q((-∞,r])\ge u\}$, using the canonical rational embedding. Assume $F$ is strictly increasing on some open interval containing $q$. Define $q_u(Q_n(y,\cdot))$ by the same convention. Then $q_u(Q_n)\to q$ in probability. The local strict-increase hypothesis permits CDFs, such as norms of nonnegative random elements, that are constant on part of $\mathbb R$.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be measurable spaces and let $y\mapsto\Pi_y$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel. For $\alpha\in[0,1]$, a set-valued rule $C$ is **graph-measurable** when
$$\{(y,\theta)\in\mathsf Y\times\Theta:\theta\in C(y)\}\in\mathcal Y\otimes\mathcal T.$$
It is a **posterior credible set at level $1-\alpha$** when it is graph-measurable and
$$\Pi_y(C(y))\ge 1-\alpha\qquad\text{for every }y\text{ in its declared data domain}.$$
The posterior-mass function is measurable by integration of the indicator of the membership graph against the kernel. If a density is available relative to a specified dominating measure, a highest-posterior-density region selects parameter values with largest density; such regions need not be intervals and may be disconnected or nonunique.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

Assume AC. Let $P_0$ have a density $f_0$ on $[0,1]$ with $\|f_0\|_\infty\le B<\infty$. Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be an orthonormal, compactly supported wavelet basis with $2^l$ coefficients at level $l\ge1$, uniformly bounded overlap, and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_\infty\le C_0 2^{l/2}$. Suppose for some $\gamma>1/2$,
$$\max_k|\langle f_0,\psi_{lk}\rangle|\le C_f2^{-l(\gamma+1/2)}.$$
Let $w_l\ge1$ be nondecreasing and admissible in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and choose either cutoff regime
$$2^{L_n}\asymp n^{1/(2\gamma+1)}\quad\text{or}\quad 2^{L_n}\asymp(n/\log n)^{1/(2\gamma+1)}.$$
For IID $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_0$, define the finite wavelet projection $P_n(L_n)$ by coefficients $\langle P_n(L_n),\psi_{lk}\rangle=P_n\psi_{lk}:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_{lk}(X_i)$ for $l\le L_n$ and zero for $l>L_n$, with the coarsest scaling coordinates projected as well. Let $G_{P_0}$ be a Borel centered Gaussian law on $M_0(w)$ whose coefficient covariance is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(G_{lk},G_{l'k'})=P_0[(\psi_{lk}-P_0\psi_{lk})(\psi_{l'k'}-P_0\psi_{l'k'})].$$
Then
$$\sqrt n\{P_n(L_n)-f_0\}\Rightarrow G_{P_0}\quad\text{in }M_0(w).$$

$X_n\to X$ in probability if and only if every subsequence of $(X_n)$ has a
further subsequence converging almost surely to $X$.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

derivations.claim: The posterior draw $f$ and center $T_n$ are $L^2$-valued, so [F2] embeds $\sqrt n(f-T_n)$ in $M_0(w)$; [F1] supplies its norm. For an $L$-Lipschitz map $T$ between metric spaces and any admissible bounded 1-Lipschitz test $h$ on its target, $h\circ T/\max(1,L)$ is an admissible test on its domain. Therefore $\beta_{BL}(T_\#\nu,T_\#\rho)\le\max(1,L)\beta_{BL}(\nu,\rho).$ By [F3], $J$ is linear and Lipschitz with a finite constant $L_J$. The bound applied pointwise to the data-indexed laws in [A1] gives $\beta_{BL}(J_\#Q_n,J_\#G_{P_0})\to0$ in probability. Moreover, if $\ell:C([0,1])\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and linear, then $\ell\circ J$ is continuous and linear on $M_0(w)$. The centered Gaussian premise on $G_{P_0}$ says exactly that this scalar pushforward is centered normal, allowing zero variance. Thus $J_\#G_{P_0}$ is a centered Gaussian Borel law. In particular, for any finite $t_1,\ldots,t_m$ and real $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, the functional $x\mapsto\sum_i a_iJx(t_i)$ is continuous and linear, so the evaluation vector $(JG_{P_0}(t_i))_{i=1}^m$ is jointly centered Gaussian. This uses only the scalar Gaussian pushforward meaning of the premise, without characteristic-function uniqueness or a Gaussian existence theorem. To identify its covariance, let $p_J1_{[0,s]}$ be the finite wavelet projection of the indicator. The finite Gaussian coefficient covariance gives $\operatorname{Cov}(J(P_JG_{P_0})(s),J(P_JG_{P_0})(t))=P_0[(p_J1_{[0,s]}-P_0p_J1_{[0,s]})(p_J1_{[0,t]}-P_0p_J1_{[0,t]})].$ By [F11], $p_J1_{[0,s]}\to1_{[0,s]}$ in Lebesgue $L^2$; since $f_0\le B$, this is also convergence in $L^2(P_0)$. The variance of a difference of two finite projected Gaussian evaluations is the $P_0$-variance of the corresponding difference of projected indicators, so it tends to zero; hence those evaluations are Cauchy in $L^2$. They also converge almost surely to $JG_{P_0}(s)$ because $P_JG_{P_0}\to G_{P_0}$ in $M_0(w)$ and $J$ is continuous. The almost-sure and in-probability limits coincide: for any $\varepsilon>0$, the probability that they differ by more than $\varepsilon$ is bounded by the two probabilities that each sequence differs from its limit by more than $\varepsilon/2$, both tending to zero. If $U_J,V_J$ are the projected evaluations and $U,V$ their $L^2$ limits, [F12] gives $|\mathbb E[U_JV_J]-\mathbb E[UV]|\le\|U_J-U\|_2\|V_J\|_2+\|U\|_2\|V_J-V\|_2\longrightarrow0;$ the norms $\|V_J\|_2$ are bounded because $V_J\to V$ in $L^2$, and the means converge to zero as well. Thus the finite covariance passes to the limit. The resulting covariance is $P_0[(1_{[0,s]}-F_0(s))(1_{[0,t]}-F_0(t))]=F_0(s\wedge t)-F_0(s)F_0(t)$, the defining covariance of the $P_0$-Brownian bridge.

The norm maps $x\mapsto\|x\|_{M(w)}$ and $F\mapsto\|F\|_\infty$ are 1-Lipschitz by the reverse triangle inequality. Applying the pushforward bound of step 1.1 first to the $M(w)$ norm and then to the supremum norm after $J$ gives bounded-Lipschitz convergence in probability of both posterior norm laws to their corresponding limit norm laws. Their CDFs satisfy [A3], so [F6] gives $R_n^M\to q_M$ and $R_n^C\to q_C$ in probability. For the projected empirical center $T_n=P_n(L_n)$, [F9] verifies [A2] under the smoothness and cutoff assumptions in [F9].

The posterior pushforward under either norm is a probability kernel on $[0,\infty)$. By [F5], the two lower quantiles are measurable and their posterior CDFs at those radii are at least $1-\alpha$. Since the centers and norms are measurable, the membership graphs of $C_n^M$ and $C_n^C$ are measurable. Thus both sets are credible by [F7].

By [A2] and [F4], $\sqrt n(T_n-f_0)\Rightarrow G_{P_0}$ and its primitive converges weakly to $B_{P_0}$. The frequentist error uses the negative center difference, but $\|f_0-T_n\|_{M(w)}=\|T_n-f_0\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|J(f_0-T_n)\|_\infty=\|J(T_n-f_0)\|_\infty$ because $J$ is linear. Thus each scaled frequentist error norm converges to the corresponding limit norm in [A3]. On the event that the random radius is within $\varepsilon$ of its deterministic limit from step 1.2, coverage is bounded above and below by probabilities for the frequentist norm with fixed thresholds expanded or contracted by $\varepsilon$. [F8] gives convergence of those fixed-threshold probabilities because [A3] makes their boundary probabilities zero. Sending $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and using the CDF value $1-\alpha$ at its quantile from [A3] yields $1-\alpha$ for both coverage probabilities. This comparison does not require independence between the data-dependent posterior radii and the frequentist center.

thm-cdf-and-multiscale-credible-band-cal.claim:
Let $P_0$ have a density $f_0$ on $[0,1]$ bounded above and bounded away from zero, and put $F_0(t)=\int_0^t f_0(x)dx$. Use the wavelet basis and $M_0(w)$ of [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and assume the wavelet conditions and summability condition $\sum_lw_l2^{-l/2}<\infty$ of [[lem-multiscale-primitive-map-to-continuous-cdfs]]. Let $T_n$ be a measurable $L^2$-valued center, let $\Pi_n$ be a posterior kernel supported on $L^2$ densities, and define $Q_n$ to be the conditional law on $M_0(w)$ of $\sqrt n(f-T_n)$ under $f\sim\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X^n)$.

Assume under $P_0^n$ that (i) $Q_n$ converges in bounded-Lipschitz distance in probability to the centered Gaussian bridge coefficient law $G_{P_0}$ in $M_0(w)$, whose finite coefficient covariances are $P_0[(h-P_0h)(g-P_0g)]$, and (ii) $\sqrt n(T_n-f_0)\Rightarrow G_{P_0}$ in $M_0(w)$. For $u=1-\alpha$, let $q_M$ and $q_C$ be the lower $u$-quantiles of $\|G_{P_0}\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|JG_{P_0}\|_\infty$. Assume both CDFs are continuous on $\mathbb R$ and strictly increasing on open neighborhoods of their respective quantiles, and that $q_M,q_C>0$. These local quantile conditions allow the CDFs to be constant on the negative half-line. $$\{(y,\theta)\in\mathsf Y\times\Theta:\theta\in C(y)\}\in\mathcal Y\otimes\mathcal T.$$
It is a **posterior credible set at level $1-\alpha$** when it is graph-measurable and
$$\Pi_y(C(y))\ge 1-\alpha\qquad\text{for every }y\text{ in its declared data domain}.$$
The posterior-mass function is measurable by integration of the indicator of the membership graph against the kernel. If a density is available relative to a specified dominating measure, a highest-posterior-density region selects parameter values with largest density; such regions need not be intervals and may be disconnected or nonunique.

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

derivations.claim: For data with $k$ successes, the likelihood is $\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}$. At $\theta_0=0$, the data are all zero with probability one, so the likelihood is $(1-\theta)^n$. For $g\in H^s_2$, $s>1/2$, and $f\in L^2([0,1])$, define $L_g(f)=\langle f,g\rangle_{L^2}$. For $x=(x_{lk})\in H(\delta)$, the intended extension is the coefficient pairing $L_g(x)=\sum_{l,k}x_{lk}\langle g,\psi_{lk}\rangle$; [[lem-smooth-functional-extends-to-negative-sobolev-space]] proves that this series is absolutely convergent and defines a continuous linear functional on $H(\delta)$ for every $\delta>0$.

lem-density-bridge-norm-cdfs-are-continu.claim:

Let $G$ be the Borel centered Gaussian bridge random element of [[lem-density-gaussian-bridge-is-borel-on-m0w]], with coefficient covariance
$$\operatorname{Cov}(G_{lk},G_{l'k'})=P_0[(\psi_{lk}-P_0\psi_{lk})(\psi_{l'k'}-P_0\psi_{l'k'})].$$
Then the distribution functions of $\|G\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|JG\|_\infty$ are continuous on $\mathbb R$ and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$. Both assign probability zero to $0$, and take values strictly between $0$ and $1$ at every positive argument. Consequently, for every $u\in(0,1)$, each has a unique positive finite lower $u$-quantile $q$, with CDF value $u$, and is strictly increasing on an open neighborhood of $q$.

Every square-summable coefficient sequence belongs to $M_0(w)$.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a compactly supported wavelet basis of [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The Haar basis with its finite scaling coordinate, as specified in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], is also allowed. Assume each level-$l$ wavelet for $l\ge l_0$ has zero integral, uniformly bounded overlap, support length at most $C_0 2^{-l}$, and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C_0 2^{-l/2}$. Let $M_0(w)$ be as in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and suppose
$$S_w:=\sum_{l\ge l_0}w_l2^{-l/2}<\infty.$$
For $x\in M_0(w)$ define
$$Jx(t):=\sum_{l,k}x_{lk}\langle 1_{[0,t]},\psi_{lk}\rangle_{L^2},\qquad 0\le t\le1.$$
Then this series converges absolutely and uniformly in $t$, $Jx\in C([0,1])$, and $\|Jx-Jy\|_\infty\le C S_w\|x-y\|_{M(w)}$ after adding the finite coarsest-level constant to $C S_w$. If $x$ is the coefficient sequence of $f\in L^2$, then $Jx(t)=\int_0^t f(u)\,du$.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for

derivations.claim: In either $E=M_0(w)$ or $E=C([0,1])$, the Borel sigma-algebra is generated by countably many continuous linear coordinates: the wavelet coordinates in the first case, and evaluations at rational times in the second. Indeed, the norm distance to a fixed point is their countable supremum, with the weights included in the first case; in the second case continuity makes the rational supremum equal the full supremum. Separability then gives a countable base of coordinate-measurable balls. Separability of $M_0(w)$ is [F1]; rational polygonal functions give a countable dense family in $C([0,1])$ by uniform continuity and finite rational approximation. Thus finite-coordinate laws determine Borel laws by [F4]. If $X$ is any centered Borel Gaussian random element in either space and $X'$ an independent copy, [F3] gives $-X\overset d=X$ and $X+X'\overset d=\sqrt2X$: every finite coordinate vector on either side is centered Gaussian with the same covariance.

For the law $\mu$ of such an $X$, let $S$ be its support, the set of points whose every open neighborhood has positive probability. Its complement is the union of all zero-mass balls in a countable base, hence has measure zero by [F5]; $S$ is closed and nonempty. Symmetry from step 1.1 gives $S=-S$. Scaling by $\sqrt2$ is a homeomorphism, so step 1.1 gives $\sqrt2S=\overline{S+S}$. Taking any $s\in S$ and $-s\in S$ shows $0\in\sqrt2S$, hence $0\in S$. Now $x+0\in\overline{S+S}=\sqrt2S$ gives $S\subseteq\sqrt2S$, while $x+x\in\sqrt2S$ gives $\sqrt2x\in S$ and hence $\sqrt2S\subseteq S$. Therefore $\sqrt2S=S$ and $\overline{S+S}=S$. This applies to $G$: any nonconstant wavelet has positive $P_0$-variance, because $f_0\ge\rho$ makes the $P_0$ and Lebesgue null sets identical and a nonconstant wavelet cannot equal a constant almost everywhere.

For each nonzero $x\in M_0(w)$, its norm is attained by some coordinate: if $r=\|x\|_{M(w)}>0$, the normalized level maxima are below $r/2$ after finitely many levels, and the maximum over the remaining finite set equals $r$. At $r=0$, the nondegenerate coordinate from step 1.3 again gives probability zero; negative values are impossible. By [F3], $Y$ and $t\mapsto\beta_{F_0(t)}$ from [F7] have the same finite Gaussian laws; step 1.1 then gives equality of their Borel laws on $C([0,1])$. Thus [F1] constructs a centered jointly Gaussian coordinate sequence $Z$ with this covariance. Each coordinate variance is at most $P_0\psi_{lk}^2\le D$.

For a centered normal of variance $v\le D$, completing the square in its normal density gives $\mathbb E e^{tZ}=e^{vt^2/2}$; at $v=0$ the variable is zero almost surely. Exponential Markov with $t=u/D$ therefore gives $\Pr(|Z|>u)\le2e^{-u^2/(2D)}$ when $D>0$, as it is for a probability density. Consequently $\Pr\{\max_k|Z_{lk}|>R\sqrt{l+1}\}\le2C2^l e^{-R^2(l+1)/(2D)}$. Choose $R$ with $R^2/(2D)>2\log2$. The sum over $l$ is finite, and the union bound over $l\ge J$ tends to zero. The probability that infinitely many of these events occur is therefore zero, since that event is contained in every such tail union.

Almost surely the normalized maxima $\max_k|Z_{lk}|/w_l$ tend to zero, by step 1.2 and admissibility $w_l/\sqrt{l+1}\to\infty$; each of the finitely many remaining coordinates is finite. The event $E=\{Z\in M_0(w)\}$ is coordinate-measurable, since the little-o condition is expressed by countable unions and intersections of the inequalities $\max_k|Z_{lk}|/w_l\le1/q$. It has probability one. Define $G=Z$ on $E$ and $G=0$ otherwise. Its finite projections are measurable finite-dimensional random elements and converge everywhere in the separable Banach space [F2]. Hence $G$ is Borel measurable: for every closed set $F$, the measurable functions $d(P_JG,F)$ converge to $d(G,F)$; inverse images of closed sets are thus measurable, and closed sets generate the Borel sigma-algebra.

Let $L$ be any continuous real linear functional on $M_0(w)$. Then $L(P_JG)\to L(G)$ almost surely, and each approximant is centered normal with some variance $v_J$. These variances are bounded. Indeed, almost-sure convergence makes the laws tight: choose $M$ so that $\Pr\{\sup_J|L(P_JG)|>M\}<1/2$, using that the supremum is finite almost surely. If $v_J\to\infty$ on a subsequence, the normal density bound would give $\Pr(|L(P_JG)|\le M)\le2M/\sqrt{2\pi v_J}\to0$, a contradiction. Any convergent subsequence of $(v_J)$ with limit $v$ gives, by [F3] and [F5], $\mathbb E e^{itL(G)}=e^{-vt^2/2}$. Taking $t=1$ shows that all subsequential variance limits coincide. Its coordinate covariance and finite Gaussian laws are unchanged by the null-set modification in step 2.1. Finally the Borel sigma-algebra of $M_0(w)$ equals the sigma-algebra generated by its countably many coordinates: the norm is their countable weighted supremum, so all open balls about a countable dense set are coordinate-measurable, and these balls generate the topology. Thus two Borel laws with the same finite-coordinate laws agree, by uniqueness of the cylinder law in [F1] restricted to this measurable space. This proves existence and uniqueness of the stated bridge law.

set of admissible counts. The evidence is
$$m(y)=\frac{n!}{\prod_jy_j!} \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j)} \frac{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j+y_j)}{\Gamma(\alpha_++n)} \in(0,\infty),$$
where $\alpha_+=\sum_j\alpha_j$, and the posterior is
$\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1+y_1,\ldots,\alpha_k+y_k)$.
For $k=1$, the parameter and count are both deterministic and the posterior
equals the prior point mass.

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

Assume AC. Let $P_0$ have density $0\le f_0\le D<\infty$ on $[0,1]$, and let $(\psi_{lk})$ be an orthonormal wavelet system with at most $C2^l$ coordinates per level, including finitely many coarsest scaling coordinates. The Haar system is allowed. For every admissible $w$, there exists a Borel centered Gaussian random element $G_{P_0}$ of $M_0(w)$ with coefficient covariance
$$K((l,k),(l',k'))=P_0[(\psi_{lk}-P_0\psi_{lk})(\psi_{l'k'}-P_0\psi_{l'k'})].$$
Its Borel law is uniquely determined by these finite-coordinate Gaussian laws.

Let $Q_n$ be data-indexed probability measures on $M_0(w)$ and let $G$ be a fixed probability measure on this space. For the projections $P_J$ of [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]], suppose that for every fixed $J$,
$$\beta_{BL}(Q_n\circ P_J^{-1},G\circ P_J^{-1})\to0$$
in probability, and that for every $\varepsilon,\eta>0$,
$$\lim_{J\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}P\left\{Q_n(\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}>\varepsilon)>\eta\right\}=0.$$
Then $\beta_{BL}(Q_n,G)\to0$ in probability.
Assume AC. A family $\mathcal A$ of Borel probabilities on a Polish space S is tight if and only if it is relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence.

Assume AC and let $k\ge0$. Let $
u$ be a finite complex Borel measure on $\mathbb R^k$. Suppose there is $\delta>0$ such that $\int e^{\delta\|x\|_1}\,|
u|(dx)<\infty$. If the Laplace transform $L(z)=\int e^{z\cdot x}\,
u(dx)$ is zero for every real $z$ in an open neighborhood of $0$, then $
u=0$.

Let $d,k,m\ge1$ be fixed. For each $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y_n\in\mathbb R^k$ be random vectors on one probability space; the probability space may vary with $n$. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ be a random vector on any probability space, and let $c\in\mathbb R^k$ be constant. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n-c=o_P(1)$, then
$$ (X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow(X,c). $$
Consequently, for every continuous $h:\mathbb R^{d+k}\to\mathbb R^m$, $h(X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow h(X,c)$. No independence between $X_n$ and $Y_n$ is required.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(S,d)$ be a Polish space, and let $\mu_n,\mu$ be Borel probability measures on $S$. Define

$$\beta_{BL}(\nu,\rho):=\sup\left\{\left|\int g\,d\nu-\int g\,d\rho\right|:g:S\to\mathbb R,\ \|g\|_\infty\le1,\ \operatorname{Lip}_d(g)\le1\right\},$$

where $\operatorname{Lip}_d(g):=\sup_{x\ne y}|g(x)-g(y)|/d(x,y)$, with value $0$ when $S$ has at most one point. Then

$$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\beta_{BL}(\mu_n,\mu)\longrightarrow0,$$

where $\Rightarrow$ is weak convergence of Borel probabilities ([[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]). The implication from bounded-Lipschitz convergence to weak convergence is choice-free; the reverse implication below uses AC through Prokhorov's theorem.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.
Every finite type-S draw and every type-H draw in [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]] is a well-defined nonnegative $L^2([0,1])$ probability density.

Use the wavelet coefficient levels $(l,k)$ and multiplicities $|K_l|=2^l$ from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The same coefficient-space definition applies to the Haar system used for type-H histograms: detail levels $l\ge0$ have $2^l$ coefficients, and the single scaling coefficient is an additional finite coarsest coordinate, included in the norm with weight $1$. Finite projections always retain that scaling coordinate; this finite convention does not alter any tail assertion. Let $w=(w_l)$ be nondecreasing with $w_l\ge1$. Define
$$M(w)=\left\{x=(x_{lk}):\|x\|_{M(w)}:=\sup_l\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}<\infty\right\}$$
and its closed little-o subspace
$$M_0(w)=\left\{x\in M(w):\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}\longrightarrow0\text{ as }l\to\infty\right\},$$
with the same norm. Call $w$ admissible when $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. The finite coarsest level is included in the norm and does not affect this limit. Elements are coefficient sequences; in particular, they need not be $L^2$ functions. [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]] proves that $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space, that $L^2$ coefficient sequences embed in it, and that finite-level projections converge in its norm.

derivations.claim: Abbreviate $m=m_n$, $a_k=a_{k,L_n}$, $A=\sum_ka_k$, $\beta_k=N_{nk}+a_k$, and $B=n+A$. The original cutoff conditions and $\alpha>1/2$ give $m/\sqrt n\to0$ and $m\log n/n\to0$, and $A\le c_2m$. On the positive simplex, the full-data histogram likelihood is $m^n\prod_k\omega_k^{N_{nk}}$. Multiplication by the prior density yields a constant times $\prod_k\omega_k^{\beta_k-1}$, with every shape positive; its normalization is finite positive by [F2]. Therefore the full-data posterior is Dirichlet$(\beta_k)_k$, regardless of whether the actual sampling truth is itself a histogram. By [F1] realize it by $\omega_k=Z_k/S$. Write $R_n$ for the posterior mean histogram measure, identified with its density in coefficient differences, with cell masses $\beta_k/B$. For a cell-constant function $q$, set $T(q)=\sum_kq_k(Z_k-\beta_k)$. Direct subtraction gives $\sqrt n(\omega q-R_nq)=(\sqrt n/S)T(q-R_nq)$.

Fix constants $t>0$ and $C$ large enough that $c:=tC-D_0(e^t-1)>0$. Since $N_{nk}$ is Binomial$(n,p_k)$ with $p_k=P_0I_{L_n,k}\le D_0/m$, independence of the observations gives $\mathbb E e^{tN_{nk}}=(1+p_k(e^t-1))^n\le e^{nD_0(e^t-1)/m}$. Hence $E_n=\{\max_kN_{nk}\le Cn/m\}$ satisfies $P_0^n(E_n^c)\le m e^{-cn/m}\to0$, by exponential Markov and the union bound. On $E_n$, for all sufficiently large $n$, $\beta_k\le C'n/m$, $B\le2n$, and both the empirical histogram density and the mean histogram density are bounded by a fixed constant $C'$ independent of $n$.

On $E_n$, take any Haar detail $\psi=\psi_{lk}$ with $l<L_n$ and put $q=\psi-R_n\psi$. Then $|q|\le2\,2^{l/2}$ and $V=\sum_k\beta_kq_k^2=B\operatorname{Var}_{R_n}(\psi)\le B R_n\psi^2\le C'n$, using $\int\psi^2=1$ and the density bound. By [F1] and [F7], $\Pr(S<B/2\mid X^n)\le4/B$, because $\operatorname{Var}(S)=B$. On the complement, step 1.1 yields $|\sqrt n(\omega\psi-R_n\psi)|\le2|T(q)|/\sqrt n$. Thus, apart from the single event $\{S<B/2\}$, the conditional probability that this absolute coefficient exceeds $x$ is at most $2\exp\{-c_0x^2/(1+2^{l/2}x/\sqrt n)\}$ for a fixed $c_0>0$. The zero-variance case has no such failure event, by [F1].

Choose a fixed $K>0$ sufficiently large. Uniformly over $l<L_n$, $2^{l/2}K\sqrt{l+1}/\sqrt n\le K\sqrt{m(L_n+1)/n}\to0$. Summing the exponential bounds of step 2.1 over levels $J<l<L_n$ and their $2^l$ coefficients therefore gives, for all large $n$, $\Pi_n\{\max_{J<l<L_n,k}|\sqrt n(f-R_n)_{lk}|/\sqrt{l+1}>K\mid X^n\}\le4/B+\sum_{l>J}2^{l+1}e^{-c_1K^2(l+1)}$ on $E_n$, with fixed $c_1>0$. The probability $4/B$ is counted only once, since the same $S$ normalizes every coordinate. Choose $K$ with $c_1K^2>2\log2$; the displayed series tail then tends to zero with $J$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, admissibility gives $K\sqrt{l+1}\le\varepsilon w_l$ for all sufficiently large $l$. Both $f$ and $R_n$ are histograms, so all their detail coordinates at $l\ge L_n$ vanish. Consequently their conditional $M(w)$ tails vanish in the iterated limit of [F4], first $n\to\infty$, then $J\to\infty$, since $P_0^n(E_n^c)\to0$.

For a Haar detail $\psi=\psi_{lk}$, exact subtraction gives $\sqrt n(R_n\psi-P_n\psi)=\sqrt n[\sum_ka_k\psi_k-A P_n\psi]/B$. Haar cell values satisfy $m^{-1}\sum_k|\psi_k|=\int|\psi|=2^{-l/2}\le1$. Hence $|\sum_ka_k\psi_k|\le c_2m$, while on $E_n$, $|P_n\psi|\le C\int|\psi|\le C$. This bounds every such mean shift by $C''m/\sqrt n\to0$. The scaling-coordinate shift is exactly zero, and all coordinates at $l\ge L_n$ vanish for both centers. Since $w_l\ge1$, $\|\sqrt n(R_n-h_n)\|_{M(w)}\to0$ uniformly on $E_n$. In particular step 2.2 also supplies the required posterior tails about $h_n$.

Fix finitely many Haar coordinates. Choose a fixed coarse dyadic partition of $r$ cells on which all their functions are constant. For large $n$ its cells are unions of level-$L_n$ cells. By [F1], the corresponding grouped Gamma variables $Z_{nj}$ are independent Gamma$(b_{nj},1)$ with $b_{nj}=N_n(J_j)+\sum_{I_{L_n,k}\subset J_j}a_k$. Their summed shape is still $B$. Write $p_j=P_0(J_j)>0$. Each coarse count satisfies $\mathbb E[N_n(J_j)/n]=p_j$ and variance at most $1/(4n)$, by observation independence. Markov applied to squared deviations, together with $A/n\to0$, proves $b_{nj}/n\to p_j$ in $P_0^n$-probability simultaneously for the fixed finite partition.

Consider any deterministic data sequence along which $b_{nj}/n\to p_j$ for every $j$. Under its conditional Gamma product laws put $Y_{nj}=(Z_{nj}-b_{nj})/\sqrt n$. For every fixed $t\in\mathbb R^r$, [F1] and the logarithm series give $\log\mathbb E e^{t\cdot Y_n}=\sum_j b_{nj}[-\log(1-t_j/\sqrt n)-t_j/\sqrt n]\to\tfrac12\sum_jp_jt_j^2$. The remainder is $O(n^{-3/2}\sum_jb_{nj}|t_j|^3)=O(n^{-1/2})$. The means of $Y_n$ are zero and their total second moments are $B/n=O(1)$, so their laws are tight by the squared-norm Markov bound and compactness of finite-dimensional closed balls. By [F5], any subsequence has a further weak limit. For any fixed $t$, the same expansion at $2t$ uniformly bounds $\mathbb E e^{2t\cdot Y_n}$; hence $e^{t\cdot Y_n}$ is uniformly integrable. Truncation of this continuous exponential therefore passes its expectation through each weakly convergent subsequence. The limit law has transform $\exp(\tfrac12\sum_jp_jt_j^2)$ and an exponential moment on a neighborhood of zero: $e^{\delta\sum_j|y_j|}\le\sum_{\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}^r}e^{\delta\epsilon\cdot y}$ and the corresponding transforms are finite. The independent centered normal vector with variances $p_j$ has this same transform, by completing the square in each normal density. Transform uniqueness [F5] identifies every subsequential limit, proving $Y_n\Rightarrow N_r(0,\operatorname{diag}(p))$.

Here $(S-B)/\sqrt n=\sum_jY_{nj}$, $S/n\to1$ in conditional probability by its variance $B/n^2\to0$ and mean $B/n\to1$. Exact algebra gives $\sqrt n(Z_{nj}/S-b_{nj}/B)=(n/S)[Y_{nj}-(b_{nj}/B)\sum_hY_{nh}]$. By [F6] and step 3.2, this vector converges to $(U_j-p_j\sum_hU_h)_j$, with $U_j$ independent $N(0,p_j)$. Its covariance is $\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^T$. Applying the fixed linear map from coarse-cell masses to the chosen Haar coordinates yields covariance exactly $P_0[(\psi-P_0\psi)(\psi'-P_0\psi')]$. Step 2.3 removes the mean shift from $R_n$ to $h_n$ on $E_n$. Thus along every deterministic data sequence with the ratios in step 3.1 converging and $E_n$ eventually occurring, the finite-coordinate posterior converges weakly, hence in BL by [F6], to the corresponding projection of [F3].

The preceding deterministic-sequence conclusion implies the finite-coordinate BL convergence in $P_0^n$-probability. To see this without a simultaneous conditional null-set assertion, if that convergence failed, there would be $\varepsilon,\eta>0$ and infinitely many $n$ with probability at least $\eta$ that the distance exceeds $\varepsilon$. Along a subsequence, step 3.1 and $P_0^n(E_n^c)\to0$ make the probability of a ratio error above $1/q$ or $E_n^c$ smaller than $\eta/2$ at its $q$th chosen index. Thus at each such index there exists data with distance above $\varepsilon$, ratio error below $1/q$, and $E_n$ true. AC selects a deterministic sequence of those data, contradicting step 3.3. This proves the asserted convergence in probability for each fixed finite projection.

The posterior histogram construction [F8] and its finite-dimensional simplex kernel make $Q_n$ a data-indexed Borel probability on $M_0(w)$: each draw and $h_n$ has only finitely many Haar coefficients, and its map from simplex coordinates is continuous. The target is the Borel bridge law [F3]. Step 3.4 supplies every fixed finite-projection BL limit, and steps 2.2–2.3 supply its posterior-tail condition. Apply [F4] to obtain the stated $M_0(w)$ BL convergence. Every original type-H assumption has been retained; in particular the lower parameter bound is compatible with, but is not needed beyond, positivity in this conjugate proof.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

derivations.claim: The finite orthogonal projection has kernel $K_L(x,y)=\sum_k\phi_{Lk}(x)\phi_{Lk}(y)$. At each $x$ only a uniformly bounded number of terms are nonzero, and each has $\|\phi_{Lk}\|_1\le C2^{-L/2}$. Thus $\int|K_L(x,y)|dy\le\sum_{k:\phi_{Lk}(x)\ne0}|\phi_{Lk}(x)|\|\phi_{Lk}\|_1\le C'$. A nonzero term requires $x,y$ to lie in one scaling support, giving the support bound. Also $K_L(x,x)=\sum_k\phi_{Lk}(x)^2\le C'2^L$; Cauchy–Schwarz on the scaling coefficients gives the claimed $L^2$ to $L^\infty$ bound.
For $h\in V_L$, $P_Lh=h$. Therefore $P_L(ah)(x)-a(x)h(x)=\int K_L(x,y)(a(y)-a(x))h(y)dy$. Hölder continuity, the support bound, and the kernel integral bound give the asserted commutator estimate.

The levelwise tail satisfies $\|\sum_k\langle g,\psi_{lk}\rangle\psi_{lk}\|_\infty\le CC_g2^{-\alpha l}$. Summing its geometric series over $l>L$ proves uniform convergence and the claimed approximation rate. Its uniform limit agrees with its $L^2$ limit, hence with $g$ almost everywhere, and everywhere for continuous representatives.

For composition put $u_j=P_jg$ and $v_j=u_j-u_{j-1}$, with the first finite low block treated as $u_0$. Levelwise derivative bounds and overlap give $\|v_j^{(q)}\|_\infty\le C_g2^{j(q-\alpha)}$ for $0\le q\le m$, and $\|u_j^{(q)}\|_\infty\le C_g^\prime2^{jq}$ for $1\le q\le m$ by summing levels; also $\sup_j\|u_j\|_\infty<\infty$. The identity $e^{u_j}-e^{u_{j-1}}=v_j\int_0^1e^{u_{j-1}+tv_j}dt$ and repeated product and chain rules therefore give, writing $H_j=e^{u_j}-e^{u_{j-1}}$, $\|H_j\|_\infty\le C2^{-j\alpha}$ and $\|H_j^{(m)}\|_\infty\le C2^{j(m-\alpha)}$. Indeed a derivative of order $q$ of the exponential factor is a finite sum of products of derivatives of its exponent of total order $q$, bounded by $C2^{jq}$; pairing with the derivative of order $m-q$ of $v_j$ gives $C2^{j(m-\alpha)}$.

The telescoping series $e^g=e^{u_0}+\sum_{j\ge1}H_j$ converges uniformly. For a wavelet at level $l$, the terms with $j\ge l$ have coefficients bounded by $C2^{-l/2}\sum_{j\ge l}2^{-j\alpha}\le C2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$. For $j<l$, subtract the degree $m-1$ Taylor polynomial of $H_j$ about a point of the wavelet support; all its integrals vanish by the stated moments. The Taylor remainder gives $|\langle H_j,\psi_{lk}\rangle|\le C2^{-l(m+1/2)}2^{j(m-\alpha)}$. Sum the geometric series over $j<l$ to get the same $C2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$ bound. The fixed smooth $e^{u_0}$ has the stronger order $2^{-l(m+1/2)}$. This proves composition in the coefficient class directly, for every positive $\alpha$ including integers, without presuming a Hölder–wavelet equivalence.

For $0<\beta<\min(\alpha,1)$ the levelwise derivative and supremum bounds for $g$ are respectively at most $C2^{j(1-\beta)}$ and $C2^{-j\beta}$. Given distance $0<\delta<1$, choose $J$ with $2^{-J-1}<\delta\le2^{-J}$. The difference of the levels through $J$ is at most $C\delta\sum_{j\le J}2^{j(1-\beta)}\le C\delta^\beta$ by the derivative bound; the remaining difference is at most $C\sum_{j>J}2^{-j\beta}\le C\delta^\beta$. Thus $g$ is $\beta$-Hölder. The exponential has bounded derivative on the bounded range of $g$, so $e^g$ has the same Hölder bound.

lem-compact-wavelet-projection-kernel-an.claim:
Let $V_L$ be the span of wavelets through level $L$ in a compactly supported orthonormal multiresolution basis on $[0,1]$, either boundary corrected or periodized. Assume constants belong to $V_L$, its dimension $d_L\asymp2^L$, and its orthonormal scaling functions $\phi_{Lk}$ have supremum norm at most $C2^{L/2}$, support diameter at most $C2^{-L}$, and uniformly bounded overlap. Periodized supports and distances are interpreted on the circle. Assume also $\sum_k|\psi_{lk}(x)|\le C2^{l/2}$ and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C2^{-l/2}$. Let $P_L$ denote the orthogonal projection onto $V_L$.

Then $P_L$ has a kernel $K_L$ satisfying $\sup_x\int|K_L(x,y)|dy\le C'$ and $K_L(x,y)=0$ when $\operatorname{dist}(x,y)>C'2^{-L}$. If $a$ is $\beta$-Hölder for $0<\beta\le1$, then
$$\|P_L(ah)-ah\|_\infty\le C'\|a\|_{C^\beta}2^{-\beta L}\|h\|_\infty,\qquad h\in V_L.$$
For the composition assertion, assume additionally an integer $m>\alpha$ such that $\|\psi_{lk}^{(q)}\|_\infty\le C_q2^{l(q+1/2)}$ for $0\le q\le m$, bounded overlap also for their derivatives, and vanishing moments through degree $m-1$ for the detail wavelets, including boundary wavelets; the finite low scaling functions are $C^m$. These are the usual sufficiently regular compact wavelet hypotheses. If a bounded function $g$ has coefficients bounded by $C_g2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$, with $\alpha>0$, and its wavelet expansion represents $g$ in $L^2$, then $\|g-P_Lg\|_\infty\le C''C_g2^{-\alpha L}$, up to equality of the continuous representatives. Under these additional derivative and cancellation hypotheses, $e^g$ also has coefficients bounded by $C_g^\prime2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$, including integer $\alpha$, and $g,e^g$ are $\beta$-Hölder for every $0<\beta<\min(\alpha,1)$. Assume AC. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID on $[0,1]$ with density $0<\rho_0\le f_0\le D_0<\infty$, and suppose $g_0=\log f_0\in C^\alpha$. Use a sufficiently regular compactly supported boundary corrected orthonormal multiresolution wavelet basis satisfying [[lem-compact-wavelet-projection-kernel-and-commutator]], with regularity greater than $\alpha$, and let $V_L$ contain exactly its wavelet levels through $L$, including the fixed low scaling space and constants. Its regularity and vanishing moments satisfy the composition hypotheses in that lemma for some integer $m>\alpha$. Let $L_n$ be either of the two cutoff sequences in [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]], fixed consistently for all $n$.
